title: Exclusive: Senate Investigation Challenges Big Tech’s Case for AI Data Centers
key_facts: A yearlong Senate investigation led by Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Chris Van Hollen and Richard Blumenthal covered Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, CoreWeave, Digital Realty and Equinix.
Several companies refused to give comprehensive permanent-employment data; some said staffing was roughly one worker per megawatt of power demand.
The most valuable incentives are sales-tax exemptions on computer equipment, not property-tax breaks; GPUs are an estimated 39% of spending at an average 1-gigawatt AI data center.

Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft all routinely sought nondisclosure agreements; Microsoft said it would stop with local governments, Amazon announced a similar policy, Google and Meta declined to commit.
None of the seven would accept a standard to pay for new power infrastructure that would not otherwise be needed.
The report cites Entergy's bid for a Richland Parish power plant tied to Meta's planned $50 billion data center; estimates say bills could rise $8-13 a month; Meta disputes responsibility.
The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3 in September; the Senate voted 57-43 against advancing it.
quote_evidence: As the world's biggest technology companies race to build data centers across the country to power an AI boom, a yearlong Senate investigation argues that some firms are misleading the public about the true costs and benefits around those projects.

The Senate investigators found none of the seven companies would agree to a standard that would require them to pay for the building of new power infrastructure that would not have been needed if not for their data centers.
Meta has disputed that its project is responsible for the costs.
why_it_matters_hint: Gives Congress findings on who pays for data center power as the issue heats up before the midterms.
notes: Report from Democratic senators' offices; TIME says findings largely match earlier press reporting.
